chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
title: Clean versus rough playing in dance and Dixieland bands
summary: Coquille describes dance-band reading versus faking jazz, his 1953 switch to Dixieland on Bourbon Street, and says he likes both clean and rough bands depending on the group.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well... That's pretty good. You know, something that occurred to me that most people don't ask about, maybe they don't think about things like this, but it strikes me that there's a difference between bands. Some play very clean and some play very rough. Now, playing with the kind of bands you did, what kind of bands do you like?

Well, as I mentioned before, I started out playing dance music and all the dance bands, well they played the regular orchestrations that you would go by at Whirline's or any of the music stores. And occasionally during the night you would fake a few tunes, you know, play some jazz, but 80% of it was reading the regular orchestrations because 90% of the work you would get was for dancing, you see. But we would throw in a few fake tunes without doing any reading at all and just kind of jazz it up a little during the night. But then, in around 1953, I switched over to the Dixieland jazz feel when I started working on Bourbon Street.

Well, some of the players I was listening to yesterday with Connie Jones, I thought they were very smooth. Well, Glenn Wilson, the new clarinet player in town, talking about him. And he'll play very smoothly for a while and then he'll play some really dirty notes, some rough style playing once in a while just to maybe lend a little variety or something. Well, that's possible.
Was he playing saxophone at the time?
No, only clarinet. Or on the clarinet?
Yeah.
And, but on the whole that was a very smooth band. Very clean. And people used to characterize Sharkey's playing as clean. Well, do you like people to play clean or rough or do you like both?

Well, it depends on the group as a whole. Yeah. How they're putting out the music. I think Connie has a, on the whole, as a clean band. I've heard his group and Connie's a wonderful trumpet player. And I'm sure he also has a few charts that have been written out, you know, and well rehearsed and well executed. And of course most of it might be played, you know, without any charts at all, which they're very capable of doing. Yeah. But I know he has some nice arrangements.
Yeah. So, you sometimes wanna hear a band that plays a little rough, gut bucket, and then sometimes smooth. Right.
It depends on the band. The voice of the band, yeah.
No rules.
Yeah. Something to get away from the usual routine of the overnight, you know, jazz.
And then somebody sits in. Keeps it from getting monotonous.
Give them a little variety. Sometimes I like bands that play out of tune and bad notes and everything, you know.
Not too bad. I can still enjoy them. Not too bad. Not too bad.
Not too bad.
Not too bad. Not too bad.
Not too often.
Well, a lot of good musicians are willing to take chances.
Well, that's true.
And they'll fluff a few notes to try a new idea.

That's true, very true, because jazz gives you the opportunity to express yourself freely, you know, and try and stay within a chord structure of that particular tune at the same time. But it gives you a chance to express your own feelings towards that particular tune that you're playing without worrying about reading music, but still staying within a chord structure of that particular number.
